title: Modern triad for magnetic material science: geometric shape, electronic bands and spin textures
authors: Denys Makarov, Oleksandr Pylypovskyi, Rui Xu, Carmine Ortix
abstract: To enable novel concepts in nanotechnologies, it is insightful to design materials with qualitatively new performances originating from recent discoveries in fundamental material science and physics. Curvilinear magnetism emerged as a tool to design chiral and anisotropic responses of materials at the nanoscale using the effects of the geometric shape and topology of the object. This concept is distinct yet complementary to material screening, which is primarily based on the optimization of intrinsic microscopic properties to modify magnetic textures for specific applications. Contemporary curvilinear magnetism focuses on mean-field micromagnetics, while the explicit contribution of the lattice structure and electronic degrees of freedom remains beyond consideration. In this review, we will emphasize on the effects which appear when this coupling is accounted for and that have resulted in novel concepts for the design of ``metageometric'' materials. Further development of this field will provide appealing technological prospects for fundamental understanding of curvilinear magnetic nanostructures and their applications in energy efficient and scalable nanoelectronics.
summary: This review outlines a modern framework for designing 'metageometric' materials by simultaneously considering the interplay between a material's physical shape, its electronic band structure, and its magnetic spin textures. It moves beyond simple micromagnetics by incorporating geometric constraints and strain effects, promising new avenues for energy-efficient nanoelectronics and sensing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need to design novel functional materials by coupling three fundamental aspects: geometric shape, electronic band structure, and magnetic spin textures.
main_result: It proposes that accounting for the explicit coupling between geometry, strain, and electronic degrees of freedom allows for the design of 'metageometric' materials with controlled anisotropic and chiral responses.
method: The review synthesizes concepts from differential geometry, mean-field micromagnetics, and solid-state physics to model these coupled effects.
model_or_system: The focus is on thin magnetic shells and curved geometries (e.g., bent shells, N-tori), where the local magnetic order parameter is influenced by the manifold's curvature and induced strain.
key_observables: Curvature-induced anisotropy, topological constraints on magnetization (soliton number), magnetoelectric coupling, and strain-gradient effects.
important_parameters: Nanoscale dimensions, curvature ($\kappa_u, \kappa_v$), strain ($\epsilon_{ij}$), and topological invariants.
main_assumptions: The review extends beyond contemporary mean-field micromagnetics to incorporate lattice structure and electronic degrees of freedom, though strain gradient effects are noted as areas for further development.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the historical development of curvilinear magnetism, geometric curvatures, and the topological constraints on magnetization fields in various curved geometries.
paper_structure: The review progresses from defining the limitations of current micromagnetics to detailing the mathematical framework using differential geometry, and finally outlining the resulting novel physical phenomena and technological prospects.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter/materials science, the explicit coupling between geometry (topology/curvature) and quantum-like order parameters (magnetization) echoes concepts in geometric phases and topological quantum matter, which are relevant to AMO physics.
